claim: 17β-estradiol (E2) decreases Kiss1 mRNA expression in Kiss1ARH neurons.
source: Since 17β-estradiol (E2) decreases Kiss1 and Tac2 mRNA expression in Kiss1ARH neurons, the role of Kiss1ARH neurons during E2-driven anorexigenic states and their coordination of POMC and NPY/AgRP feeding circuits have been largely ignored.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background knowledge and is later confirmed by experimental data in Figure 2A.

claim: 17β-estradiol (E2) decreases Tac2 mRNA expression in Kiss1ARH neurons.
source: Since 17β-estradiol (E2) decreases Kiss1 and Tac2 mRNA expression in Kiss1ARH neurons, the role of Kiss1ARH neurons during E2-driven anorexigenic states and their coordination of POMC and NPY/AgRP feeding circuits have been largely ignored.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background knowledge and is later confirmed by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: E2 augmented the excitability of Kiss1ARH neurons by amplifying Cacna1g, Hcn1 and Hcn2 mRNA expression.
source: Presently, we show that E2 augmented the excitability of Kiss1ARH neurons by amplifying Cacna1g, Hcn1 and Hcn2 mRNA expression and T-type calcium and h-currents.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data showing increased mRNA expression (Figure 2A) and electrophysiological measurements showing increased currents (Figure 2B).

claim: E2 augmented the excitability of Kiss1ARH neurons by amplifying T-type calcium and h-currents.
source: Presently, we show that E2 augmented the excitability of Kiss1ARH neurons by amplifying Cacna1g, Hcn1 and Hcn2 mRNA expression and T-type calcium and h-currents.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements showing increased current densities in E2-treated animals (Figure 2B).

claim: E2 increased Slc17a6 mRNA expression in Kiss1ARH neurons.
source: E2 increased Slc17a6 mRNA expression and glutamatergic synaptic input to arcuate neurons, which excited POMC and inhibited NPY/AgRP neurons via metabotropic receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data showing approximately 2-fold higher levels of Slc17a6 mRNA in E2-treated animals (Figure 3).

claim: E2 increased glutamatergic synaptic input to arcuate neurons.
source: E2 increased Slc17a6 mRNA expression and glutamatergic synaptic input to arcuate neurons, which excited POMC and inhibited NPY/AgRP neurons via metabotropic receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by paired-pulse ratio experiments showing increased probability of glutamate release in E2-treated animals (Figure 5).

claim: Glutamatergic input from Kiss1ARH neurons excited POMC neurons via metabotropic receptors.
source: E2 increased Slc17a6 mRNA expression and glutamatergic synaptic input to arcuate neurons, which excited POMC and inhibited NPY/AgRP neurons via metabotropic receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation experiments showing high-frequency stimulation generated slow EPSCs in POMC neurons that were blocked by mGluR antagonists (Figure 7).

claim: Glutamatergic input from Kiss1ARH neurons inhibited NPY/AgRP neurons via metabotropic receptors.
source: E2 increased Slc17a6 mRNA expression and glutamatergic synaptic input to arcuate neurons, which excited POMC and inhibited NPY/AgRP neurons via metabotropic receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation experiments showing high-frequency stimulation generated slow IPSCs in NPY/AgRP neurons (Figure 7).

claim: Deleting Slc17a6 in Kiss1 neurons eliminated glutamate release.
source: Deleting Slc17a6 in Kiss1 neurons eliminated glutamate release and led to conditioned place preference for sucrose in E2-treated KO female mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic experiments showing no fast glutamatergic responses in POMC, NPY/AgRP, and Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons from KO animals (Figure 12).

claim: Deleting Slc17a6 in Kiss1 neurons led to conditioned place preference for sucrose in E2-treated KO female mice.
source: Deleting Slc17a6 in Kiss1 neurons eliminated glutamate release and led to conditioned place preference for sucrose in E2-treated KO female mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral experiments showing that E2-treated KO mice developed a preference for the sucrose-paired chamber (Figure 16A).

claim: The E2-driven increase in Kiss1 neuronal excitability and glutamate neurotransmission may play a key role in governing the motivational drive for palatable food in females.
source: Therefore, the E2-driven increase in Kiss1 neuronal excitability and glutamate neurotransmission may play a key role in governing the motivational drive for palatable food in females.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the integration of electrophysiological and behavioral findings.

claim: Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons are essential for positive feedback by estradiol on gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neuronal activity and the luteinizing hormone (LH) surge in rodents.
source: Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons are essential for positive feedback by estradiol on gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neuronal activity and the luteinizing hormone (LH) surge in rodents (Clarkson et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clarkson et al., 2008.

claim: 17β-estradiol (E2) increases Kiss1 mRNA expression in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons.
source: 17β-estradiol (E2) increases Kiss1 mRNA expression in these rostral Kiss1 neurons (Smith et al., 2005), and their excitability is increased by the E2-driven upregulation of T-type calcium, hyperpolarization-activated, cyclic-nucleotide gated (h)- and persistent sodium (INaP) currents (Piet et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2015,2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2005.

claim: The excitability of Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons is increased by the E2-driven upregulation of T-type calcium, hyperpolarization-activated, cyclic-nucleotide gated (h)- and persistent sodium (INaP) currents.
source: 17β-estradiol (E2) increases Kiss1 mRNA expression in these rostral Kiss1 neurons (Smith et al., 2005), and their excitability is increased by the E2-driven upregulation of T-type calcium, hyperpolarization-activated, cyclic-nucleotide gated (h)- and persistent sodium (INaP) currents (Piet et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2015,2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Piet et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2015, 2013.

claim: Glutamate induces burst firing and pacemaking activity in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons.
source: In addition, glutamate induces burst firing and pacemaking activity in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons (Wang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: E2 significantly inhibits Kiss1 mRNA expression in ARH neurons.
source: In contrast to the Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons, E2 significantly inhibits Kiss1 mRNA expression in ARH neurons (Lehman et al., 2010; Navarro et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lehman et al., 2010; Navarro et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2005.

claim: Kiss1ARH neurons co-express the peptide neurotransmitters kisspeptin (Kiss1), tachykinin 2 (Tac2; a.k.a. neurokinin B; NKB) and dynorphin.
source: Kiss1ARH neurons co-express the peptide neurotransmitters kisspeptin (Kiss1), tachykinin 2 (Tac2; a.k.a. neurokinin B; NKB) and dynorphin (Lehman et al., 2013), which have been proposed to be responsible for pulsatile release of GnRH and LH (Clarkson et al., 2017; Li et al., 2009; Navarro et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lehman et al., 2013.

claim: Kisspeptin, Tac2, and dynorphin have been proposed to be responsible for pulsatile release of GnRH and LH.
source: Kiss1ARH neurons co-express the peptide neurotransmitters kisspeptin (Kiss1), tachykinin 2 (Tac2; a.k.a. neurokinin B; NKB) and dynorphin (Lehman et al., 2013), which have been proposed to be responsible for pulsatile release of GnRH and LH (Clarkson et al., 2017; Li et al., 2009; Navarro et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Clarkson et al., 2017; Li et al., 2009; Navarro et al., 2009.

claim: The cellular mechanisms by which Kiss1ARH neurons synchronize to drive GnRH pulses involves a combination of co-released Tac2 excitation via Tac3 receptors and dynorphin presynaptic inhibition via κ-opioid receptors.
source: Indeed, the cellular mechanisms by which Kiss1ARH neurons synchronize to drive GnRH pulses was recently elucidated and involves a combination of co-released Tac2 excitation via Tac3 receptors and dynorphin presynaptic inhibition via κ-opioid receptors (Qiu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Qiu et al., 2016.

claim: Kiss1ARH neurons express the vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (vGluT2).
source: Kiss1ARH neurons also express the vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (vGluT2) (Cravo et al., 2011; Nestor et al., 2016), an indication that they have the potential to package and release the neurotransmitter glutamate (Herman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cravo et al., 2011; Nestor et al., 2016.

claim: Expression of vGluT2 indicates that Kiss1ARH neurons have the potential to package and release the neurotransmitter glutamate.
source: Kiss1ARH neurons also express the vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (vGluT2) (Cravo et al., 2011; Nestor et al., 2016), an indication that they have the potential to package and release the neurotransmitter glutamate (Herman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Herman et al., 2014 and is based on established knowledge about vGluT2 function.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Kiss1ARH neurons evokes glutamatergic EPSCs in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons.
source: Optogenetic activation of Kiss1ARH neurons evokes glutamatergic EPSCs not only in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons (Qiu et al., 2016) but also in proopiomelanocortin (POMC) and neuropeptide Y/agouti-related peptide (NPY/AgRP) neurons (Nestor et al., 2016), which further establishes direct functional connections between Kiss1ARH neurons and hypothalamic neurons important for the control of reproduction and energy homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Qiu et al., 2016.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Kiss1ARH neurons evokes glutamatergic EPSCs in proopiomelanocortin (POMC) and neuropeptide Y/agouti-related peptide (NPY/AgRP) neurons.
source: Optogenetic activation of Kiss1ARH neurons evokes glutamatergic EPSCs not only in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons (Qiu et al., 2016) but also in proopiomelanocortin (POMC) and neuropeptide Y/agouti-related peptide (NPY/AgRP) neurons (Nestor et al., 2016), which further establishes direct functional connections between Kiss1ARH neurons and hypothalamic neurons important for the control of reproduction and energy homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nestor et al., 2016.

claim: In males, Slc17a6 mRNA and glutamate release are increased in gonadectomized as compared to intact animals.
source: In males, Slc17a6 (encodes vGluT2) mRNA and glutamate release are increased in gonadectomized as compared to intact animals, an indication of inhibitory effects of gonadal steroids on glutamate neurotransmission in these neurons (Nestor et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nestor et al., 2016.

claim: Gonadal steroids have inhibitory effects on glutamate neurotransmission in Kiss1ARH neurons in males.
source: In males, Slc17a6 (encodes vGluT2) mRNA and glutamate release are increased in gonadectomized as compared to intact animals, an indication of inhibitory effects of gonadal steroids on glutamate neurotransmission in these neurons (Nestor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that gonadectomy increases Slc17a6 mRNA and glutamate release.

claim: There are pronounced male/female differences in feeding behavior.
source: Based on pronounced male/female differences in feeding behavior and the excitatory glutamatergic input from Kiss1ARH neurons to Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons in females (Asarian and Geary, 2006; Qiu et al., 2016), we hypothesized that the mRNA expression of Slc17a6 and glutamate release in females in contrast to males, would be amplified by E2 in Kiss1ARH neurons in order to help maintain reproduction during different energy states.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Asarian and Geary, 2006.

claim: Tac2 mRNA was the most highly expressed in Kiss1ARH neurons from OVX females.
source: Based on the CT values (Figure 1) and quantitative analysis with Tacr3 as calibrator (see Materials and Methods), Tac2 mRNA was the most highly expressed in Kiss1ARH neurons from OVX females, such that Tac2 >>> (50-fold) Pdyn ≥Kiss1 >> (6-fold) Slc17a6, and with E2 treatment, Tac2 >> (18-fold) Pdyn >> (2-fold) Slc17a6 > (2-fold) Kiss1 (one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1 and quantitative analysis.

claim: In OVX females, Tac2 mRNA expression is 50-fold higher than Pdyn and Kiss1, and 6-fold higher than Slc17a6 in Kiss1ARH neurons.
source: Based on the CT values (Figure 1) and quantitative analysis with Tacr3 as calibrator (see Materials and Methods), Tac2 mRNA was the most highly expressed in Kiss1ARH neurons from OVX females, such that Tac2 >>> (50-fold) Pdyn ≥Kiss1 >> (6-fold) Slc17a6, and with E2 treatment, Tac2 >> (18-fold) Pdyn >> (2-fold) Slc17a6 > (2-fold) Kiss1 (one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of qPCR data shown in Figure 1.

claim: With E2 treatment, Tac2 mRNA expression is 18-fold higher than Pdyn, 2-fold higher than Slc17a6, and 2-fold higher than Kiss1 in Kiss1ARH neurons.
source: Based on the CT values (Figure 1) and quantitative analysis with Tacr3 as calibrator (see Materials and Methods), Tac2 mRNA was the most highly expressed in Kiss1ARH neurons from OVX females, such that Tac2 >>> (50-fold) Pdyn ≥Kiss1 >> (6-fold) Slc17a6, and with E2 treatment, Tac2 >> (18-fold) Pdyn >> (2-fold) Slc17a6 > (2-fold) Kiss1 (one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of qPCR data shown in Figure 1.

claim: E2 increased the mRNA expression of Cacna1g in Kiss1ARH neurons from E2-treated females as compared to oil-treated, OVX females.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the mRNA expression of Cacna1g and Hcn1 and Hcn2 were significantly increased in Kiss1ARH neurons from E2-treated females as compared to oil-treated, OVX females (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: E2 increased the mRNA expression of Hcn1 in Kiss1ARH neurons from E2-treated females as compared to oil-treated, OVX females.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the mRNA expression of Cacna1g and Hcn1 and Hcn2 were significantly increased in Kiss1ARH neurons from E2-treated females as compared to oil-treated, OVX females (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: E2 increased the mRNA expression of Hcn2 in Kiss1ARH neurons from E2-treated females as compared to oil-treated, OVX females.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the mRNA expression of Cacna1g and Hcn1 and Hcn2 were significantly increased in Kiss1ARH neurons from E2-treated females as compared to oil-treated, OVX females (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Kiss1 mRNA levels were significantly reduced by E2 in Kiss1ARH neurons.
source: For comparison we also measured Kiss1 and Pdyn mRNAs in the same neuronal pools, and as predicted, Kiss1 and Pdyn mRNA levels were significantly reduced by E2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Pdyn mRNA levels were significantly reduced by E2 in Kiss1ARH neurons.
source: For comparison we also measured Kiss1 and Pdyn mRNAs in the same neuronal pools, and as predicted, Kiss1 and Pdyn mRNA levels were significantly reduced by E2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Both T- and h-currents were increased in Kiss1ARH neurons with E2-treatment as compared to oil-treatment.
source: In addition, both T- and h-currents (Figure 2B) as well as neuronal excitability (measured as rebound excitation; Figure 2C) were increased in Kiss1ARH neurons with E2-treatment as compared to oil-treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Neuronal excitability (measured as rebound excitation) was increased in Kiss1ARH neurons with E2-treatment as compared to oil-treatment.
source: In addition, both T- and h-currents (Figure 2B) as well as neuronal excitability (measured as rebound excitation; Figure 2C) were increased in Kiss1ARH neurons with E2-treatment as compared to oil-treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Although E2-treatment downregulates neuropeptide expression in Kiss1ARH neurons, it significantly increases the intrinsic conductances and hence the excitability of these vital neurons.
source: Therefore, although E2-treatment downregulates neuropeptide expression in Kiss1ARH neurons, it significantly increases the intrinsic conductances and hence the excitability of these vital neurons.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Kiss1ARH neurons in E2-treated, OVX female mice expressed approximately 2-fold higher levels of Slc17a6 mRNA than oil-treated, OVX mice.
source: The qPCR analysis revealed that Kiss1ARH neurons (5 cells/pool; 3–6 pools/animal) in E2-treated, OVX female mice expressed approximately 2-fold higher levels of Slc17a6 mRNA than oil-treated, OVX mice (Figure 3), while the level of Slc32a1 mRNA was undetectable in Kiss1ARH neurons from both groups of female mice (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The level of Slc32a1 mRNA was undetectable in Kiss1ARH neurons from both oil-treated and E2-treated OVX female mice.
source: The qPCR analysis revealed that Kiss1ARH neurons (5 cells/pool; 3–6 pools/animal) in E2-treated, OVX female mice expressed approximately 2-fold higher levels of Slc17a6 mRNA than oil-treated, OVX mice (Figure 3), while the level of Slc32a1 mRNA was undetectable in Kiss1ARH neurons from both groups of female mice (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on qPCR data that showed Slc32a1 mRNA was below the level of detectability.

claim: The mRNA expression of Tac2 was significantly reduced in E2-treated females compared to oil-treated females.
source: For comparison we also measured Tac2 and Tacr3 mRNAs in the same Kiss1ARH neuronal pools, and as expected, the mRNA expression of these transcripts were both significantly reduced in E2-treated females (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The mRNA expression of Tacr3 was significantly reduced in E2-treated females compared to oil-treated females.
source: For comparison we also measured Tac2 and Tacr3 mRNAs in the same Kiss1ARH neuronal pools, and as expected, the mRNA expression of these transcripts were both significantly reduced in E2-treated females (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The E2-induced increased Slc17a6 mRNA expression in Kiss1ARH neurons is an indication that the amino acid neurotransmitter glutamate is regulated differently by E2 than the neuropeptides in females.
source: Therefore, the E2-induced increased Slc17a6 mRNA expression in Kiss1ARH neurons is an indication that the amino acid neurotransmitter glutamate is regulated differently by E2 than the neuropeptides in females.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential regulation of Slc17a6 (increased) versus neuropeptides (decreased) by E2.

claim: Seventy-seven cells showed an inward current following photostimulation with a mean amplitude of 29.8 ± 3.4 pA, a mean latency to peak of 4.0 ± 0.1 ms, and an average decay time constant of 5.5 ± 0.6 ms.
source: In total, seventy-seven cells showed an inward current following photostimulation with a mean amplitude of 29.8 ± 3.4 pA, a mean latency to peak of 4.0 ± 0.1 ms, and an average decay time constant of 5.5 ± 0.6 ms.
evidence: This claim is based on electrophysiological measurements from optogenetic experiments.

claim: The light-induced response in POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons was blocked with the AMPA- and NMDA-receptor blockers, CNQX and AP5, respectively.
source: This light-induced response was blocked with the AMPA- and NMDA-receptor blockers, CNQX and AP5, respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Glutamate, and not GABA, is the primary amino acid neurotransmitter released from Kiss1ARH neurons in females.
source: Therefore, glutamate, and not GABA, is the primary amino acid neurotransmitter released from Kiss1ARH neurons in females.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that the light-induced response was blocked by glutamate receptor antagonists.

claim: TTX abrogated the photostimulated post-synaptic inward current in POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons, but the light-induced response could be rescued with the addition of the potassium channel blocker 4-AP.
source: Moreover, although TTX (1 μM) abrogated the photostimulated post-synaptic inward current, we could rescue the light-induced response with the addition of the potassium channel blocker 4-AP (100 μM to the bath) in both POMC (n = 3) and NPY/AgRP (n = 2) neurons (Figure 4D,E), which is biophysical evidence for direct synaptic signaling from Kiss1ARH neurons to POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons (Cousin and Robinson, 2000; Petreanu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: The rescue of the light-induced response with 4-AP is biophysical evidence for direct synaptic signaling from Kiss1ARH neurons to POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: Moreover, although TTX (1 μM) abrogated the photostimulated post-synaptic inward current, we could rescue the light-induced response with the addition of the potassium channel blocker 4-AP (100 μM to the bath) in both POMC (n = 3) and NPY/AgRP (n = 2) neurons (Figure 4D,E), which is biophysical evidence for direct synaptic signaling from Kiss1ARH neurons to POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons (Cousin and Robinson, 2000; Petreanu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the electrophysiological data supported by citations to Cousin and Robinson, 2000; Petreanu et al., 2009.

claim: There was no difference in the amplitude of the evoked fast PSCs between POMC and NPY neurons.
source: Based on this analysis, there was no difference in the amplitude of the evoked fast PSCs between POMC and NPY neurons (post-hoc identified) (25.8 ± 4.8 pA, n = 36 POMC neurons versus 33.3 ± 4.9 pA, n = 41 NPY/AgRP neurons).
evidence: This claim is based on electrophysiological measurements comparing POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons.

claim: When Kiss1ARH neurons in the female are firing at low frequencies there is equivalent fast (ionotropic) glutamatergic input to both POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons in the female, similar to what we found in males.
source: Therefore, it appears that when Kiss1ARH neurons in the female are firing at low frequencies there is equivalent fast (ionotropic) glutamatergic input to both POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons in the female, similar to what we found in males (Nestor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electrophysiological data and comparison to previous findings in males.

claim: POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons in E2-treated, OVX female mice had a significantly lower PPR compared to oil-treated, OVX females.
source: Using a photostimulation PPR protocol of two 5 ms LED stimulations separated by 50 ms (Figure 5A,B), we found that POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons in E2-treated, OVX female mice had a significantly lower PPR compared to oil-treated, OVX females in both POMC neurons (Figure 5C,D) and in NPY/AgRP neurons (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by paired-pulse ratio experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: A lower PPR indicates that there is a greater probability of glutamate release with the first stimulus in E2-treated, OVX animals.
source: These results indicate that there is a greater probability of glutamate release with the first stimulus in E2-treated, OVX animals (Figure 5B), which is consistent with higher mRNA expression of Slc17a6 in Kiss1ARH neurons following E2-treatment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the paired-pulse ratio data based on established principles of synaptic physiology.

claim: The lower PPR in E2-treated animals is consistent with higher mRNA expression of Slc17a6 in Kiss1ARH neurons following E2-treatment.
source: These results indicate that there is a greater probability of glutamate release with the first stimulus in E2-treated, OVX animals (Figure 5B), which is consistent with higher mRNA expression of Slc17a6 in Kiss1ARH neurons following E2-treatment.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the electrophysiological findings to the molecular data.

claim: There is a striking male/female difference concerning the effects of sex steroids (testosterone versus estradiol) on Slc17a6 mRNA expression and glutamate release in Kiss1ARH neurons.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that there is a striking male/female difference concerning the effects of sex steroids (testosterone versus estradiol) on Slc17a6 mRNA expression and glutamate release in Kiss1ARH neurons (Nestor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current findings in females and previous findings in males cited from Nestor et al., 2016.

claim: ChR2-mCherry injections labeled Kiss1ARH neurons within the arcuate nucleus only.
source: Currently we confirmed that ChR2-mCherry injections labeled Kiss1ARH neurons within the arcuate nucleus only (Figure 6A1), and sent extensive fiber-projections rostrally to the AVPV/PeN area in the vicinity of immunoreactive Kiss1 neurons (Figure 6A2,A3).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 6A1.

claim: ChR2-mCherry labeled Kiss1ARH neurons sent extensive fiber-projections rostrally to the AVPV/PeN area in the vicinity of immunoreactive Kiss1 neurons.
source: Currently we confirmed that ChR2-mCherry injections labeled Kiss1ARH neurons within the arcuate nucleus only (Figure 6A1), and sent extensive fiber-projections rostrally to the AVPV/PeN area in the vicinity of immunoreactive Kiss1 neurons (Figure 6A2,A3).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 6A2,A3.

claim: ChR2-mCherry expressing cell bodies were not found in the AVPV/PeN.
source: Notably, ChR2-mCherry expressing cell bodies were not found in the AVPV/PeN.
evidence: This is an observation from the immunocytochemistry experiments.

claim: Photostimulation-induced an inward current in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons, which was blocked in the presence of TTX but rescued with addition of 4-AP in the presence of TTX.
source: Photostimulation-induced an inward current in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons, which was blocked in the presence of TTX (1 μM) but rescued with addition of 4-AP in the presence of TTX (n = 4) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The rescue of the photostimulation-induced inward current with 4-AP is biophysical evidence for direct synaptic signaling from Kiss1ARH neurons to Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons.
source: Therefore, this is biophysical evidence for direct synaptic signaling from Kiss1ARH neurons to Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the electrophysiological data based on established principles.

claim: AVPV/PeN neurons from E2-treated females had reduced PPR, an indication that Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons receive an enhanced glutamatergic input from Kiss1ARH neurons in E2-treated females.
source: Using a photoactivation-PPR protocol of two 5 ms LED stimulations as described above, we found that AVPV/PeN neurons, including Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons, from E2-treated females had reduced PPR, an indication that Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons, similar to POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons, receive an enhanced glutamatergic input from Kiss1ARH neurons in E2-treated females (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by paired-pulse ratio experiments shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: High-frequency (20 Hz) stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons generated a slow EPSC in POMCEGFP neurons.
source: High-frequency (20 Hz) stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons/fibers generated a slow EPSC in POMCEGFP neurons, and in current clamp the stimulation depolarized POMC neurons and increased their firing rate (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: High-frequency stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons depolarized POMC neurons and increased their firing rate.
source: High-frequency (20 Hz) stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons/fibers generated a slow EPSC in POMCEGFP neurons, and in current clamp the stimulation depolarized POMC neurons and increased their firing rate (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: High-frequency optogenetic stimulation generated a slow IPSC in NPYGFP neurons.
source: In contrast, high-frequency optogenetic stimulation generated a slow IPSC in NPYGFP neurons, and in current clamp the same stimulus hyperpolarized and inhibited NPY neurons (Figure 7A,D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: High-frequency stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons hyperpolarized and inhibited NPY neurons.
source: In contrast, high-frequency optogenetic stimulation generated a slow IPSC in NPYGFP neurons, and in current clamp the same stimulus hyperpolarized and inhibited NPY neurons (Figure 7A,D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The high frequency response in NPY/AgRP neurons was blocked approximately 90% by the mGluR7 antagonist ADX71743.
source: This high frequency response was blocked approximately 90% by the mGluR7 antagonist ADX71743 (IPSP reduced from 5.9 ± 1.2 mV to 0.6 ± 0.2 mV, n = 5; paired t-test, t(4) = 4.281, p=0.013).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments with the mGluR7 antagonist.

claim: The change in membrane potential following Kiss1ARH stimulation was significantly different between POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: The change in membrane potential following Kiss1ARH stimulation was significantly different between POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: High-frequency activity in Kiss1ARH neurons, which through presumably glutamate spillover to extrasynaptic mGluRs, excites POMC but inhibits NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: Therefore, high-frequency activity in Kiss1ARH neurons, which through presumably glutamate spillover to extrasynaptic mGluRs (Nietz et al., 2017; Watanabe and Nakanishi, 2003), excites POMC but inhibits NPY/AgRP neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electrophysiological data and supported by citations to Nietz et al., 2017; Watanabe and Nakanishi, 2003.

claim: POMC neurons expressed group I metabotropic glutamate receptor, mGluR1 and/or mGluR5.
source: This analysis revealed that POMC neurons expressed group I metabotropic glutamate receptor, mGluR1 and/or mGluR5 (mGluR1, 44%, n = 5 animals; mGluR5, 21%, n = 5 animals) (Figure 8A,B), whereas NPY/AgRP neurons expressed primarily the group III metabotropic glutamate receptors, mGluR7, with a few neurons also expressing the group II mGluR2 (mGluR7, 50%, n = 5 animals; mGluR2, 13%; n = 4 animals) (Figure 8C,D).

claim: NPY/AgRP neurons expressed primarily the group III metabotropic glutamate receptors, mGluR7, with a few neurons also expressing the group II mGluR2.
source: This analysis revealed that POMC neurons expressed group I metabotropic glutamate receptor, mGluR1 and/or mGluR5 (mGluR1, 44%, n = 5 animals; mGluR5, 21%, n = 5 animals) (Figure 8A,B), whereas NPY/AgRP neurons expressed primarily the group III metabotropic glutamate receptors, mGluR7, with a few neurons also expressing the group II mGluR2 (mGluR7, 50%, n = 5 animals; mGluR2, 13%; n = 4 animals) (Figure 8C,D).

claim: DHPG (50 μM) depolarized and stimulated firing in POMC neurons.

evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: DHPG induced an inward current in synaptically-isolated POMC neurons.
source: Therefore, we used the mGluR 1/5 agonist DHPG (3,5-dihydroxyphenylglycine) to explore its action in POMC neurons, and found that DHPG (50 μM) depolarized and stimulated firing in POMC neurons (Figure 9A), and induced an inward current in synaptically-isolated POMC neurons (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The I-V relationship for the DHPG-induced current showed a reversal at −30 mV, indicating that a cationic current was driving the pronounced depolarization.

claim: There was no difference in the depolarizing effects of DHPG on POMC neurons in oil-treated as compared to E2-treated, OVX females.

claim: DHPG had no effect on NPY/AgRP neurons.

claim: DCG-IV (10 µM) hyperpolarized and inhibited firing in NPY neurons.

claim: DCG-IV induced an outward current in NPY/AgRP neurons in the presence of fast sodium channel, ionotropic glutamatergic and GABAergic blockade.

claim: The I-V relationship for the DCG-IV induced current exhibited inward rectification and a reversal potential at EK+ (−95 mV), the hallmark of activation of G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying K+ (GIRK) channels.
source: The I-V relationship for the DCG-IV induced current exhibited inward rectification and a reversal potential at EK+ (−95 mV), the hallmark of activation of G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying K+ (GIRK) channels (Figure 10C).
evidence: This claim is supported by I-V relationship data shown in Figure 10C and is based on established knowledge about GIRK channels.

claim: 10 µM DCG-IV was more efficacious to hyperpolarize NPY/AgRP neurons in E2-treated OVX females, indicating that there was a more robust E2-induced inhibition of NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: Moreover, 10 µM DCG-IV was more efficacious to hyperpolarize NPY/AgRP neurons in E2-treated OVX females, indicating that there was a more robust E2-induced inhibition of NPY/AgRP neurons (Figure 10G).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 10G.

claim: DCG IV had no effect on POMC neuronal excitability.
source: DCG IV, however, had no effect on POMC neuronal excitability (data not shown).

claim: AMN082 (10 µM) hyperpolarized and inhibited firing in NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: Since mGluR7 was the most highly expressed in NPY/AgRP neurons (Figure 8), we also tested the mGluR7-selective agonist AMN082 (10 µM) (Ren et al., 2011) for its postsynaptic actions on NPY/AgRP neurons. Indeed, AMN082 hyperpolarized and inhibited firing in NPY/AgRP neurons (Figure 10D).

claim: AMN082 generated about a 2-fold greater outward current than DCG-IV, which reversed near EK+.
source: It generated about a 2-fold greater outward current than DCG-IV, which reversed near EK+ (Figure 10E,F), and the magnitude of the hyperpolarization was significantly increased in E2-treated, OVX females (Figure 10H).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 10E,F.

claim: The magnitude of the hyperpolarization induced by AMN082 was significantly increased in E2-treated, OVX females.
source: It generated about a 2-fold greater outward current than DCG-IV, which reversed near EK+ (Figure 10E,F), and the magnitude of the hyperpolarization was significantly increased in E2-treated, OVX females (Figure 10H).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 10H.

claim: AMN082 (10 µM) had no effect on a POMC neuron that exhibited a robust response to DHPG.
source: However, AMN082 (10 µM) had no effect on a POMC neuron that exhibited a robust response to DHPG (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on electrophysiological experiments, though the data are not shown.

claim: The mRNA expression of mGluR7 was significantly increased in NPY neurons obtained from E2- versus oil-treated OVX females.
source: In addition, the mRNA expression of mGluR7 was significantly increased in NPY neurons obtained from E2- versus oil-treated OVX females (Figure 10I).

claim: E2 significantly increases the receptor expression and response of NPY/AgRP to group II/III mGluR's (Gi,o-coupled), which would contribute to the inhibition of these orexigenic neurons in heightened E2-driven reproductive states.
source: Therefore, E2 significantly increases the receptor expression and response of NPY/AgRP to group II/III mGluR's (Gi,o-coupled), which would contribute to the inhibition of these orexigenic neurons in heightened E2-driven reproductive states.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electrophysiological and molecular data.

claim: None of the YFP cells in KO females expressed Slc17a6, whereas 100% expressed Tac2.

claim: High-frequency optogenetic stimulation generated a similar slow EPSP amplitude in arcuate Kiss1 neurons from oil-treated, OVX Kiss1 control and oil-treated OVX Slc17a6 KO Kiss1 mice.

evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 11C,D,G.

claim: High-frequency optogenetic stimulation of Kiss1 neurons in E2-treated, OVX control and E2-treated, OVX Slc17a6 KO mice revealed a significantly reduced slow EPSP in Slc17a6 KO as compared to control Kiss1ARH neurons.

evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 11E,F,G.

claim: Even though the slow EPSP is generated mainly by Tac2 in OVX females, glutamate may contribute to the slow EPSP in Kiss1ARH neurons in E2-treated, OVX females.
source: Therefore even though the slow EPSP is generated mainly by Tac2 in OVX females (Qiu et al., 2016), glutamate may contribute to the slow EPSP in Kiss1ARH neurons in E2-treated, OVX females.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electrophysiological data and previous findings cited from Qiu et al., 2016.

claim: Low-frequency optogenetic stimulation (0.5 Hz) failed to evoke a fast glutamatergic postsynaptic response in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons from female Kiss1CreGFP::Slc17a6lox/∆ mice.

claim: Low-frequency optogenetic stimulation (0.5 Hz) failed to evoke a fast glutamatergic postsynaptic response in POMC neurons from female Kiss1CreGFP::Slc17a6lox/∆ mice.
source: Therefore, we used whole-cell, voltage-clamp recordings in Kiss1AVPV/PeN, POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons from female Kiss1CreGFP::Slc17a6lox/∆ mice and found that low-frequency optogenetic stimulation (0.5 Hz) failed to evoke a fast glutamatergic postsynaptic response in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons (Figure 12C), POMC neurons (Figure 12E) or NPY/AgRP neurons (Figure 12G).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 12E.

claim: Low-frequency optogenetic stimulation (0.5 Hz) failed to evoke a fast glutamatergic postsynaptic response in NPY/AgRP neurons from female Kiss1CreGFP::Slc17a6lox/∆ mice.
source: Therefore, we used whole-cell, voltage-clamp recordings in Kiss1AVPV/PeN, POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons from female Kiss1CreGFP::Slc17a6lox/∆ mice and found that low-frequency optogenetic stimulation (0.5 Hz) failed to evoke a fast glutamatergic postsynaptic response in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons (Figure 12C), POMC neurons (Figure 12E) or NPY/AgRP neurons (Figure 12G).

claim: High-frequency stimulation (20 Hz, 10 s) evoked a small residual inward current (2.8 ± 0.3 pA, n = 7) in POMC neurons from E2-treated, OVX KO females.

claim: High-frequency stimulation (20 Hz, 10 s) evoked a small outward current (4.0 ± 1.6 pA, n = 4) in NPY/AgRP neurons from E2-treated, KO females.

claim: The evoked postsynaptic responses in POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons from KO females following high-frequency stimulation were generated by kisspeptin release.

evidence: This is a speculation based on previous findings cited from Fu and van den Pol, 2010 and the absence of glutamate release in KO animals.

claim: Kisspeptin (200 nM) inhibited firing and hyperpolarized NPYGFP neurons even in the presence of the GABAA blocker bicuculline (10 μM).

claim: Similar to the GABAB receptor agonist baclofen, kisspeptin induced an outward, albeit smaller current with a reversal potential close to EK+ (−90 mV).

claim: Kisspeptin binds to and activates neuropeptide FF receptors 1 and 2 (NPFFR1 and NPFFR2).
source: In addition to binding to the Kiss1 receptor (GPR54), kisspeptin is also known to bind to and activate neuropeptide FF receptors 1 and 2 (NPFFR1 and NPFFR2), and these Gαi/o coupled receptors are both expressed in the ARH (Elhabazi et al., 2013; Rønnekleiv et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Elhabazi et al., 2013; Rønnekleiv et al., 2014.

claim: NPFFR1 and NPFFR2 are Gαi/o coupled receptors that are both expressed in the ARH.
source: In addition to binding to the Kiss1 receptor (GPR54), kisspeptin is also known to bind to and activate neuropeptide FF receptors 1 and 2 (NPFFR1 and NPFFR2), and these Gαi/o coupled receptors are both expressed in the ARH (Elhabazi et al., 2013; Rønnekleiv et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Elhabazi et al., 2013; Rønnekleiv et al., 2014.

claim: Npffr1 mRNA is expressed in NPY neurons.

claim: RFRP-3 (10 μM), a selective agonist for NPFFR1 and NPFFR2, hyperpolarized and inhibited the firing of NPY/AgRP neurons.

claim: The I/V plot of the RFRP-3 induced current showed a reversal potential close to EK+ (−85 mV).
source: The I/V plot of the RFRP-3 induced current showed a reversal potential close to EK+ (−85 mV) (Figure 13F).
evidence: This claim is supported by I-V relationship data shown in Figure 13F.

claim: It is probable that kisspeptin and RFRP3 activate the same receptor on NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: Therefore, it is probable that kisspeptin and RFRP3 activate the same receptor on NPY/AgRP neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar electrophysiological effects of kisspeptin and RFRP-3.

claim: Kiss1r mRNA (GPR54) is expressed in a subpopulation of POMC neurons.
source: We also explored the actions of kisspeptin on POMC neurons after first identifying that Kiss1r mRNA (GPR54) is expressed in a subpopulation of these neurons using scRT-PCR (Figure 14A).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data shown in Figure 14A.

claim: Kisspeptin (200 nM) depolarized and increased the firing frequency of POMC neurons.
source: In agreement with a previous publication (Fu and van den Pol, 2010), we found that kisspeptin (200 nM) depolarized and increased the firing frequency of POMC neurons (Figure 14B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 14B and a citation to Fu and van den Pol, 2010.

claim: The I/V plot showed that kisspeptin activated a non-selective cationic channel that reversed at −10 mV in POMC neurons.
source: In addition, the I/V plot showed that kisspeptin activated a non-selective cationic channel that reversed at −10 mV (Figure 14C).
evidence: This claim is supported by I-V relationship data shown in Figure 14C.

claim: Ad libitum access to standard, low-fat mouse chow did not affect body weight in mice lacking Slc17a6 in Kiss1 neurons versus control females over the limited time-course of the study.
source: Ad libitum access to standard, low-fat mouse chow did not affect body weight in mice lacking Slc17a6 in Kiss1 neurons versus control females over the limited time-course of our study (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on body weight measurements, though the data are not shown.

claim: E2-treated, OVX Kiss1 female mice failed to exhibit a change in place preference for sucrose.
source: Food-motivated, behavioral analysis revealed that E2-treated, OVX Kiss1 female mice failed to exhibit a change in place preference for sucrose, a natural food reward (Figure 16A, Figure 16—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 16A and Figure 16—figure supplement 1.

claim: E2-treated, OVX Slc17a6 KO mice significantly increased their occupancy of the sucrose-paired chamber.
source: In contrast, E2-treated, OVX Slc17a6 KO mice significantly increased their occupancy of the sucrose-paired chamber (Figure 16A).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 16A.

claim: E2-treated, OVX Heterozygous (Slc17a6+/lox::Kiss1CreGFP/+) mice showed a trend to increase their occupancy in the sucrose-paired chamber.
source: E2-treated, OVX Heterozygous (Slc17a6+/lox::Kiss1CreGFP/+) mice showed a trend to increase their occupancy in the sucrose-paired chamber (Figure 16A).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 16A.

claim: The E2-treated, OVX Kiss1 controls did not increase their sucrose intake at any time.
source: In addition, we measured the amount of sucrose consumed by each experimental group during conditioning. The E2-treated, OVX Kiss1 controls did not increase their sucrose intake at any time (Figure 16B, Figure 16—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 16B and Figure 16—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Slc17a6 KO females slightly increased their sucrose intake on day 6 of the test (third day of sucrose exposure) and this was significantly augmented by day 8 of the test (fourth day of sucrose exposure).
source: The Slc17a6 KO females slightly increased their sucrose intake on day 6 of the test (third day of sucrose exposure; Figure 15) and this was significantly augmented by day 8 of the test (fourth day of sucrose exposure) (Figure 16B, Figure 15).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 16B.

claim: The Slc17a6 Het mice exhibited a smaller, but significant increase in sucrose consumption on day 6 of the test.
source: The Slc17a6 Het mice exhibited a smaller, but significant increase in sucrose consumption on day 6 of the test (Figure 16B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 16B.

claim: E2-treated, OVX Kiss1 control females had a consistent diminished motivation for sucrose, whereas abolishing glutamate release from Kiss1 neurons enhanced the motivational response for sucrose.
source: Together, these findings indicate that E2-treated, OVX Kiss1 control females had a consistent diminished motivation for sucrose, whereas abolishing glutamate release from Kiss1 neurons enhanced the motivational response for sucrose.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral data from the CPP experiments.

claim: Attenuating glutamate release from Kiss1 neurons in Slc17a6 Het females nearly recapitulated the phenotype of the Slc17a6 KO animals suggesting a gene-dosage/threshold effect.
source: Interestingly, attenuating glutamate release from Kiss1 neurons in Slc17a6 Het females nearly recapitulated the phenotype of the Slc17a6 KO animals suggesting a gene-dosage/threshold effect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data comparing Het and KO animals.

claim: Although both the Slc17a6 KO and Het mice gained weight in comparison to the E2-treated, OVX Kiss1 controls, the difference was only statistically significant in the Slc17a6 Het mice.
source: Although both the Slc17a6 KO and Het mice gained weight in comparison to the E2-treated, OVX Kiss1 controls, the difference was only statistically significant in the Slc17a6 Het mice (Figure 16C).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 16C.

claim: Slc17a6 mRNA in Het mice was ~35% of that of controls.
source: As illustrated (Figure 16D), Slc17a6 mRNA in Het mice was ~35% of that of controls (Slc17a6 Het mice, 5 pools each from 4 animals; Kiss1 control mice, 5 pools each from 5 animals), and Slc17a6 mRNA was not detected in Kiss1 neurons from Slc17a6 KO females.

claim: Slc17a6 mRNA was not detected in Kiss1 neurons from Slc17a6 KO females.

evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 16D.

claim: Intact males, which have reduced Slc17a6 mRNA expression in Kiss1ARH neurons and reduced glutamate release compared to castrates and E2-treated females, demonstrated a motivation for sucrose based on CPP.
source: Interestingly intact males, which have reduced Slc17a6 mRNA expression in Kiss1ARH neurons and reduced glutamate release compared to castrates (Nestor et al., 2016) and E2-treated females, demonstrated a motivation for sucrose based on CPP (Figure 16—figure supplement 1).

claim: The estrous cycle was normal in Slc17a6 KO females.

evidence: This claim is supported by estrous cycle monitoring data.

claim: The time to conception when placed with a fertile male was not different between wild type, Het, and KO groups.
source: Similarly, the time to conception when placed with a fertile male was not different between the three groups (one-way ANOVA; p=0.68 comparing time (days) to conception between: WT, n = 9, 1.75 ± 0.40; Het, n = 3, 2.83 ± 1.64; KO, n = 8, 1.89 ± 0.67).
evidence: This claim is supported by fertility measurements.

claim: The peptide neurotransmitters in Kiss1ARH neurons are negatively regulated by E2.
source: It is well known that the peptide neurotransmitters in Kiss1ARH neurons are negatively regulated by E2, and these neurons are responsible for pulsatile release of GnRH and reproduction (Oakley et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Oakley et al., 2009 and is established knowledge.

claim: Kiss1ARH neurons are responsible for pulsatile release of GnRH and reproduction.
source: It is well known that the peptide neurotransmitters in Kiss1ARH neurons are negatively regulated by E2, and these neurons are responsible for pulsatile release of GnRH and reproduction (Oakley et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Oakley et al., 2009 and is established knowledge.

claim: E2 increases the expression of Slc17a6 and glutamate release, revealing that the amino acid and peptide neurotransmitters are regulated differentially by E2 in Kiss1ARH neurons in females in contrast to findings in males.
source: Our current findings that E2 increases the expression of Slc17a6 and glutamate release reveal that the amino acid and peptide neurotransmitters are regulated differentially by E2 in Kiss1ARH neurons in females in contrast to our findings in males (Nestor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the current findings and comparison to previous findings in males.

claim: E2 increased the expression of T-type calcium and h-currents in female Kiss1ARH neurons, which led to increased neuronal excitability, concomitant with E2-induced inhibition of the expression of the peptide neurotransmitter mRNAs Kiss1, Tac2 and Pdyn.
source: We also found that E2 increased the expression of T-type calcium and h-currents in female Kiss1ARH neurons, which led to increased neuronal excitability, concomitant with E2-induced inhibition of the expression of the peptide neurotransmitter mRNAs Kiss1, Tac2 and Pdyn.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the electrophysiological and molecular data presented.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Kiss1ARH neurons revealed direct frequency-dependent glutamatergic and peptidergic neurotransmission to POMC and AgRP neurons in females, an indication that Kiss1ARH neurons may play a role in regulating feeding behavior.
source: Optogenetic activation of Kiss1ARH neurons revealed direct frequency-dependent glutamatergic and peptidergic neurotransmission to POMC and AgRP neurons in females, an indication that Kiss1ARH neurons may play a role in regulating feeding behavior.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the optogenetic experiments and is a speculation about the role of Kiss1ARH neurons.

claim: The glutamatergic outputs were lost in females with conditional ablation of Slc17a6 in Kiss1ARH neurons, whereas excitatory and inhibitory kisspeptin responses could be evoked in POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons, respectively.
source: The glutamatergic outputs were lost in females with conditional ablation of Slc17a6 in Kiss1ARH neurons, whereas excitatory and inhibitory kisspeptin responses could be evoked in POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons, respectively.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the optogenetic and pharmacological experiments in KO animals.

claim: Slc17a6 KO females did not gain weight on normal mouse chow, but the motivation to ingest sucrose was increased in females lacking vGluT2 in Kiss1 neurons.
source: Experiments in vivo revealed that Slc17a6 KO females did not gain weight on normal mouse chow, but the motivation to ingest sucrose was increased in females lacking vGluT2 in Kiss1 neurons.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the behavioral experiments.

claim: Kiss1ARH neurons may provide E2- and frequency- dependent signals not only to POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons, but also to Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons to help coordinate feeding and reproduction in females.
source: Overall, these and other findings support the idea that Kiss1ARH neurons may provide E2- and frequency- dependent signals not only to POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons, but also to Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons to help coordinate feeding and reproduction in females (Figure 17).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the integration of all the findings and is illustrated in Figure 17.
